body_markdown:
Say you’re building a segment of mid-market software companies with 50 to 200 employees and a specific revenue band. The attributes you’re filtering on, industry, size, revenue, location, ownership, are firmographic data, and they’re the backbone of any account-based approach. This guide covers what firmographic data actually includes, how it stacks up against technographic and behavioral segmentation, and how to keep those fields from going out of date.


**TLDR:**


- Firmographic data covers industry, headcount, revenue, location, and ownership structure for companies.
- Technographic data identifies software and infrastructure a company uses or has recently used, found through website code, DNS records, and job postings.
- Firmographic segmentation filters large lists down to accounts worth calling, often paired with behavioral or intent signals for timing.
- Appended firmographic data decays as companies grow, get acquired, or rebrand, so re-verify fields on a quarterly cadence.
- PredictLeads tracks firmographic attributes, including industry classification via NAICS codes, through its Companies dataset.


## What Is Firmographic Data?


Firmographic data is the set of organization-level attributes, industry, size, revenue, location, and structure, that B2B teams use to profile and categorize companies. It is the business equivalent of demographics, except it describes a company instead of a person.


The firmographic meaning traces back to industrial marketing research from the 1970s and 1980s, when scholars needed a way to segment organizations the way marketers already segmented individual consumers. The term is sometimes called emporographics or firm demographics, blending “demographics” with “geographics.” These firmographic synonyms all point to the same concept: structural facts about a company, not the people inside it.


## Firmographic Data Examples


Firmographic data breaks down into a handful of recurring categories, each useful for a different segmentation task.


- Industry classification: North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) or Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes group companies by what they do, so you can target “software publishers” instead of guessing from a name.
- Company size: Headcount separates a 10 person startup from a 10,000 person enterprise. Of 6.4 million US companies with paid employees, 89 percent had fewer than 20, and only 21,041 had 500 or more, per the[Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2022/econ/susb/2022-susb-annual.html) .
- Annual revenue: Shows whether a company can afford your product, apart from headcount.
- Location: Headquarters and branch sites drive territory assignment and outreach timing.
- Ownership structure: Public, private, or subsidiary status changes who approves the deal.
- Funding stage: A company fresh off a Series B has budget a bootstrapped firm may not.


## Firmographic Data vs Demographic Data


Demographic data describes a person: age, income, education, job title. Firmographic data describes the organization that person works for: industry, size, revenue, location. In B2B, a job title shows who can approve a purchase, while firmographics show whether the employer is a plausible buyer at all. A VP of Sales at a 10 person startup behaves differently from one at a 5,000 person enterprise, even with the same title.

## Firmographic Data vs Technographic Data


Firmographic data and technographic data answer different questions about the same account. Firmographic data describes what a company is: its industry, headcount, revenue, and location. Technographic data describes what a company uses: its CRM, cloud host, and the rest of its software stack. A sales team might filter firmographically to land on mid-market software companies in a specific revenue band, then layer in technographic data to see which of those accounts already use, or have recently used, a complementary tool or a competitor’s product. The two approaches pair well because firmographics narrow a broad market to a workable account list, while technographics add tech-stack context that firmographics alone cannot show. The section below defines technographic data on its own terms before comparing how each approach supports segmentation differently.


## What Is Technographic Data?


[Technographic data](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data/) identifies which software, hosting, and infrastructure a company uses, from CRM platform to cloud host. Providers detect this through[technographic data collection methods](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data-collection-methods) such as website code, DNS records, cookies, and job postings, together offering evidence of tools a company uses or has recently used.


In marketing, technographic segmentation applies that detection to targeting: group companies by tech stack instead of size or industry, since your product may only matter to companies that use, or have recently used, a complementary or competing tool.


[Technographic data providers](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data-providers/) split into specialists and bundled suites like ZoomInfo, which tracks technology usage across more than[30 million companies](https://ir.zoominfo.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zoominfo-provides-technology-usage-insights-more-30-million/) .


## Firmographic Segmentation Explained


Firmographic segmentation groups companies by shared traits so sales and marketing teams can rank and tailor messaging by segment instead of treating every account the same.


Most B2B teams segment along four axes:


- Industry: group by NAICS code, since a healthcare buyer and a logistics buyer face different problems.
- Company size: headcount ranges separate startups from enterprises, since buying processes differ sharply at each tier.
- Revenue band: isolates companies that can plausibly afford your price point.
- Location: supports territory assignment and timezone-aware outreach.


A worked example: a sales team might define a segment as mid-market software companies in North America with 50 to 200 employees, then add a revenue band of 5 million to 50 million dollars. That filter stack cuts a list of thousands down to the accounts worth calling first, each segment getting its own message and priority score.


## Firmographic Segmentation vs Psychographic and Behavioral Segmentation


Firmographic segmentation groups companies by structural traits. Psychographic segmentation groups decision-makers by values, culture, or attitudes, things like risk tolerance or how a buying committee views vendor consolidation. Behavioral segmentation groups prospects by observed actions: website visits, content downloads, demo requests, past purchases. Demographic segmentation applies at the individual buyer level, job title, seniority, tenure, distinct from company-level firmographics even though the two often get paired.

Firmographics tell you which companies belong on a list, not who on that list is paying attention right now. Most mature B2B programs layer firmographic targeting with behavioral or intent signals, an approach covered in depth in[account-based marketing technographic data](https://predictleads.com/blog/account-based-marketing-technographic-data/) , instead of picking one type alone.


## Why Firmographic Data Matters for B2B Sales and Marketing


Firmographic data turns a vague target market into a workable account list. A rep can rule out companies outside the right revenue band or industry in seconds, instead of researching each one by hand. RevOps uses the same attributes to split territories fairly, and marketing matches messaging to context, since a pitch built for a 20 person startup rarely lands with a 5,000 person enterprise.


This is also the backbone of account-based marketing, where campaigns target a defined list instead of a wide net, often built using[technographic data for ABM](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data-for-abm-and-how-to-build-target-account-lists/) alongside firmographic filters. The global account-based marketing market was valued at 1.4 billion dollars in 2024, is estimated to reach 1.9 billion dollars in 2026, and is projected to reach 3.8 billion dollars by 2030, growing at a compound annual rate of 17.9 percent, according to[Grand View Research](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/account-based-marketing-market-report) .


## Where to Find Firmographic and Technographic Data


Teams sourcing firmographic and technographic data typically pick from four paths, each with a different tradeoff between cost, coverage, and freshness.


- Public and government databases: business registries, census data, and regulatory filings are free and authoritative, but update slowly and vary in format across jurisdictions.
- Third-party data vendors: these aggregate company records at scale, trading some accuracy for broad coverage. Methodology differs, so two vendors can report different headcounts for the same company, a gap closely tied to[technographic data accuracy](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data-accuracy/) issues across providers.
- Primary research: surveys and outreach produce the most current data for a narrow set of accounts, but do not scale past a few hundred companies.
- API-based access: delivers structured records directly into a CRM or data warehouse for teams that need continuous refresh instead of a one-time pull.


A one-time market sizing exercise can lean on public sources. A sales team scoring live leads needs a vendor or API with regular refresh cycles instead, which is why it helps to know[how to choose a technographic data provider](https://predictleads.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-technographic-data-provider/) before committing budget.


## How to Append and Maintain Accurate Firmographic Data


Firmographic data append matches an existing record, usually by domain or company name, against a reference database to fill in missing fields like revenue range, employee count, industry code, and location.


A few habits keep appended data usable:


- Re-verify on a set cadence, such as quarterly, instead of treating an append as a one-time task.
- Cross-check fields against more than one source, since a single vendor’s methodology can misjudge headcount or revenue.
- Watch match keys closely. Name variants, website redirects, and subsidiaries under a parent company cause silent mismatches.


Domain-based matching holds up better than name matching, since a domain stays fixed while names vary across sources.

## Final Thoughts on Using Firmographic Data in B2B


Good account targeting starts with firmographic basics but gets stronger once you layer in technographic and behavioral signals. You don’t need every data point, just the ones that actually change how you rank and talk to accounts. Keep your sources cross-checked and your append cadence consistent, and your list stays worth working. ## FAQ


### What is firmographic data in simple terms?


Firmographic data is a set of organization-level facts, industry, headcount, revenue, location, and ownership structure, used to describe and categorize a company. It is the B2B equivalent of demographic data for individuals, and it typically comes from firmographic data providers, company registries, or direct firmographic data append against your existing records.


### Firmographic data vs technographic data: which should I use for targeting?


Use firmographic data to decide which companies belong on your list (industry, size, revenue band) and technographic data to decide which of those companies are a fit based on their tech stack. Most B2B teams combine both: firmographic segmentation narrows a market to a workable account list, then technographic segmentation (via a technology detections dataset tracking tools like Salesforce or HubSpot) flags which accounts use a complementary or competing product.


### How does ZoomInfo technographic data compare to a specialized technographic data provider?


ZoomInfo bundles technographic data with firmographic and contact data, tracking technology usage across more than 30 million companies, which suits teams that want one vendor for everything. A specialized technographic data provider that detects technologies through script tags, DNS records, cookies, and job postings can offer more source transparency into how and where each detection was found, which matters when you need evidence for a competitor displacement or integration-targeting play.


### What is firmographic segmentation and how do I build a segmentation example?


Firmographic segmentation groups companies by shared structural traits, industry, headcount, revenue, and location, so you can rank and message each segment differently instead of treating every account the same. A typical firmographic segmentation b2b example: mid-market software companies in North America with 50 to 200 employees and 5 million to 50 million dollars in revenue, which narrows a list of thousands down to the accounts worth calling first.


### Can I get alerted when a target account posts a new job opening or raises funding?


Yes. A company intelligence API that tracks Job Openings and Financing Events as separate datasets lets you query or receive webhook notifications when a followed company posts a new role or shows a` receives_financing` event, instead of manually checking a careers page or news feed. This turns hiring and funding activity, two of the strongest firmographic data examples of account momentum, into timed outreach triggers instead of static profile fields.
